power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: Inter-trial intervals assign time costs to actions during learning
table.description:
Background 
Classic reinforcement learning models, such as the Rescorla - Wagner model, focus primarily on reward: whether outcomes are better or worse than expected, and how value estimates should be updated accordingly. However, when participants engage in decision-making tasks, a key component of real-world choice is often overlooked - time. Time spent on a given action is time not spent on alternatives, making it a meaningful opportunity cost that may shape behavior.
While prior work has shown that fatigue and prolonged task engagement can alter decision-making processes over time, it remains largely unclear whether the fine-grained temporal structure of a task - specifically inter-trial intervals (ITIs) - systematically influences learning and choice. Similar to how individuals learn expected value from reward feedback, they may also learn expectations about time based on ITI feedback, and integrate these estimates to maximize reward rate per unit time.
In a prior study from our lab, we directly tested this idea using a three-armed restless bandit task in which ITI duration (1s vs. 4s) was manipulated within-subject. Across two experiments (N = 100 each), we found that longer ITIs increased the likelihood of switching away from the previously selected option, suggesting that participants assign a cost to actions that precede longer delays. To account for this effect, we developed a series of computational models and showed that participants maintain separate expectations over reward and time, integrating them at the moment of decision. In particular, an ITI Learn model—incorporating dynamically updated time expectations and time prediction errors—provided the best fit to behavior, outperforming competing models. In that study, the effect was observed in both task variants (with and without a perceptual distractor during the ITI), though it was somewhat stronger in the no-distractor version. Accordingly, the present study adopts the no-distractor version to maximize sensitivity to the effect. Given its superior fit and its ability to capture ITI-dependent modulation of choice, the ITI Learn model is expected to provide a strong account of behavior in the current data as well.
Building on these findings, the current study tests whether ITIs influence decision policies in a general adult sample, and whether individual differences in transdiagnostic traits modulate this effect. We focus on impulsivity and anhedonia, as they make distinct - and partially opposing - predictions regarding sensitivity to time costs. First, we aim to replicate the core finding that longer ITIs increase switching behavior. Second, we predict that impulsivity will be positively associated with the magnitude of this ITI effect, reflecting heightened sensitivity to delays. Third, we predict that anhedonia will be negatively associated with the ITI effect, reflecting reduced sensitivity to temporal differences. As an exploratory analysis, we may also examine an interaction between impulsivity and anhedonia, although primary analyses will focus on these associations separately.
Participants
A total of 472 adult participants will be recruited via Prolific. All participants will provide informed consent and self-confirm no history of neurological or psychiatric diagnoses. Sample size was determined based on planned power analyses for the primary correlational hypotheses. 
Replicating main effect: Longer ITI promotes switching away from last action. 
Power was estimated by parametric Monte-Carlo simulation. Reference fixed- and random-effects parameters were obtained by fitting the planned generalised linear mixed model
is_shift ~ 1 + prev_ITI + (1 + prev_ITI | subject), family = binomial(logit),
to combined pilot data from two studies (N = 180 subjects, 17,627 trials, after excluding subjects performing at or below chance). The fitted ITI fixed-effect was b = 0.074 in log-odds per second of inter-trial interval (Wald SE = 0.012, LRT χ²(1) = 33.5, p = 7.1 × 10⁻⁹; parametric-bootstrap LRT p < 0.001, 1000 simulations; profile-likelihood 95% CI [0.050, 0.098]). The estimated random-effects covariance was used as-is (intercept SD = 0.91, slope SD = 0.073, r = −0.30).
For each of 100 simulated samples of N = 472 subjects, trial counts per subject and the proportion of long-ITI trials per subject were drawn (with replacement) from the empirical distribution; subject-specific intercepts and slopes were drawn from the estimated random-effects MVN; trial-level shift responses were generated under the fitted logistic GLMM. Each simulated dataset was fit with the full model and with a nested null model omitting the prev_ITI fixed effect, and inference was carried out using a likelihood-ratio test (preferred over Wald because Wald is anti-conservative in GLMMs). Power was defined as the proportion of simulations with LRT p < .05.
At N = 472, estimated power for the ITI effect was >0.99 (100/100 simulations significant; median simulated p = 6.3 × 10⁻²¹).
Individual differences
Specifically, using a one-tailed correlation test with α = .05, power = .95, and an assumed effect size of r = .15, G*Power estimated a required sample size of 472 participants.
Task Design
Participants will complete a 100-trial, three-armed restless bandit task in which the reward probabilities of each arm drift gradually according to a fixed random-walk process. The key manipulation is ITI length, varied within-subjects across short and long intervals. After each choice and reward feedback, the next trial begins after the assigned interval. We use the no-distractor version of the task, in which no perceptual filler appears during the ITI, since prior results showed a slightly stronger effect under this condition, although the effect was present in both variants.
Measures
Behavioral measures will include choice patterns across trials, switching rates (stay versus shift behavior), and reaction times. Participants will also complete self-report questionnaires assessing impulsivity and anhedonia, which we treat as transdiagnostic traits rather than categorical diagnoses.
Modeling Approach
We will compare a baseline Rescorla–Wagner model against ITI-augmented alternatives. The primary model is the ITI Learn model described above, which won the model comparison in our prior anxiety study and which we therefore expect to provide the best account here as well. To assess robustness, we will run a sensitivity analysis and apply an updated modeling procedure that allows different best-fitting models per participant rather than enforcing a single model across the sample.

table.title: Replication new ITI sequence effect of ITI on bandit RL learning
table.research_questions:
WE have the same core hypothesis - that longer ITI promotes switching in a 3-armed bandit task - and here like our 3 previous studies (https://osf.io/6tmja/ most recent and highlights prior two studies), we use the same task and reward trajectory. We simply alter the ITI sequence. We will use the same mixed model as before, except now control for trial number influencing switching rate (since we later observed switching declines over the task). WE will do so both using frequentists and bayesian methods for sensitivity analysis to show findings our robust to this methods choice. 

We seek to replicate our primary hypothesis in a study n=132. This is slightly greater than the our original studies with n=100, to deal with potential drop-out rates.
table.foreknowledge_of_data_or_evidence: Data does not yet exist. No part of the data that will be used for this analysis plan exists, and no part will be generated until after this plan is registered.
table.study_type: Randomized Experiment: Must include random assignment of subjects to treatments or conditions. This usually includes lab experiments, field experiments, intervention experiments, randomized controlled trials, and A/B testing.
table.intention_for_causal_interpretation: Direct inference on causal relationship(s): This study is intended to infer or estimate a causal relationship between two or more variables. It is designed specifically for the purposes of causal inference or identification.
table.study_design_overview: see https://osf.io/6tmja/ except here ITI sequence is changed so that 52% of trials in first half of trials are 1s (as opposed to the longer ITI which is 4s). s is seconds.
table.data_collection_procedures: Collecting on Prolific from English-speaking countries. Made sure participants did not participate in any earlier version of this project.
table.sample_size_rationale: Over-powered for previous main effect (n=100) due to ITI-sequence change which might slightly mitigate the effect.
table.manipulated_variables: ITI is the main manipulated variable - ensure some ITIs are 1s and some are 4s (each 50% representation in our 100-trial task, now slightly more 1s early on).
table.measured_variables: Sensitivity of choice-switching to ITI length, controlling for trial number.
table.indices:
Mixed-effects models. Every mixed-effects regression was fitted as a Bayesian model in PyMC by the No-U-Turn sampler (nutpie; 4 chains × 1,000 draws after 1,000 warm-up iterations, target acceptance 0.9; github_repo/analysis_common/bayes_glmm.py). The preregistered model was extended by a linear effect of trial number, which absorbs the decline in switching over the session:
logit P(switch_ij) = (β0 + u0,j) + (βITI + uITI,j) · ITI_ij + (βT + uT,j) · trial_ij
where ITI_ij is the prior ITI of participant j's choice i in seconds and trial_ij is the trial number centred and scaled per 50 trials ((t − 50.5)/50), each entering as a fixed effect and a participant-level random slope. Other contrasts (for example a long interval after the choice two trials back) enter in the same way, with the trial term in every model. Priors were N(0, 1.5) on the intercept, N(0, 1) on the other fixed effects and half-normal(1) on the random-effect standard deviations. The random effects were independent: the random interval slope varies little between participants, so its correlations with the other random effects were not identified and did not mix. We report the posterior mean, the 95% credible interval (CrI), the odds ratio for 4 s against 1 s, and the two-sided posterior tail probability, 2 × min(P(β > 0), P(β < 0)), in place of a p value. Every model reported has R̂ ≤ 1.1 for its fixed effects and random-effect standard deviations. Effects after wins and after losses were estimated in those trials separately, and their difference by the prior ITI × previous outcome interaction in all trials.

In particular, an ITI Learn model—incorporating dynamically updated time expectations and time prediction errors—provided the best fit to behavior, outperforming competing models. In that study, the effect was observed in both task variants (with and without a perceptual distractor during the ITI), though it was somewhat stronger in the no-distractor version. Accordingly, the present study adopts the no-distractor version to maximize sensitivity to the effect. Given its superior fit and its ability to capture ITI-dependent modulation of choice, the ITI Learn model is expected to provide a strong account of behavior in the current data as well.
Building on these findings, the current study tests whether ITIs influence decision policies in a general adult sample, and whether individual differences in transdiagnostic traits modulate this effect. We focus on impulsivity and anhedonia, as they make distinct - and partially opposing - predictions regarding sensitivity to time costs. First, we aim to replicate the core finding that longer ITIs increase switching behavior. Second, we predict that impulsivity will be positively associated with the magnitude of this ITI effect, reflecting heightened sensitivity to delays. Third, we predict that anhedonia will be negatively associated with the ITI effect, reflecting reduced sensitivity to temporal differences. As an exploratory analysis, we may also examine an interaction between impulsivity and anhedonia, although primary analyses will focus on these associations separately.
Participants
A total of 472 adult participants will be recruited via Prolific. All participants will provide informed consent and self-confirm no history of neurological or psychiatric diagnoses. Sample size was determined based on planned power analyses for the primary correlational hypotheses.
Replicating main effect: Longer ITI promotes switching away from last action.
Power was estimated by parametric Monte-Carlo simulation. Reference fixed- and random-effects parameters were obtained by fitting the planned generalised linear mixed model
is_shift ~ 1 + prev_ITI + (1 + prev_ITI | subject), family = binomial(logit),
to combined pilot data from two studies (N = 180 subjects, 17,627 trials, after excluding subjects performing at or below chance). The fitted ITI fixed-effect was b = 0.074 in log-odds per second of inter-trial interval (Wald SE = 0.012, LRT χ²(1) = 33.5, p = 7.1 × 10⁻⁹; parametric-bootstrap LRT p < 0.001, 1000 simulations; profile-likelihood 95% CI [0.050, 0.098]). The estimated random-effects covariance was used as-is (intercept SD = 0.91, slope SD = 0.073, r = −0.30).
For each of 100 simulated samples of N = 472 subjects, trial counts per subject and the proportion of long-ITI trials per subject were drawn (with replacement) from the empirical distribution; subject-specific intercepts and slopes were drawn from the estimated random-effects MVN; trial-level shift responses were generated under the fitted logistic GLMM. Each simulated dataset was fit with the full model and with a nested null model omitting the prev_ITI fixed effect, and inference was carried out using a likelihood-ratio test (preferred over Wald because Wald is anti-conservative in GLMMs). Power was defined as the proportion of simulations with LRT p < .05.
At N = 472, estimated power for the ITI effect was >0.99 (100/100 simulations significant; median simulated p = 6.3 × 10⁻²¹).
Individual differences
Specifically, using a one-tailed correlation test with α = .05, power = .95, and an assumed effect size of r = .15, G*Power estimated a required sample size of 472 participants.
Task Design
Participants will complete a 100-trial, three-armed restless bandit task in which the reward probabilities of each arm drift gradually according to a fixed random-walk process. The key manipulation is ITI length, varied within-subjects across short and long intervals. After each choice and reward feedback, the next trial begins after the assigned interval. We use the no-distractor version of the task, in which no perceptual filler appears during the ITI, since prior results showed a slightly stronger effect under this condition, although the effect was present in both variants.
Measures
Behavioral measures will include choice patterns across trials, switching rates (stay versus shift behavior), and reaction times. Participants will also complete self-report questionnaires assessing impulsivity and anhedonia, which we treat as transdiagnostic traits rather than categorical diagnoses.
Modeling Approach
We will compare a baseline Rescorla–Wagner model against ITI-augmented alternatives. The primary model is the ITI Learn model described above, which won the model comparison in our prior anxiety study and which we therefore expect to provide the best account here as well. stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. stat_effect_size.summary_text: We found 33 t-tests and/or F-tests where effect sizes are not reported. Check these tests in the table below, and consider adding effect sizes.

table.text: In Study 1, participants switched away from the option they had just chosen on 45.1% of trials after a 4 s ITI versus 38.9% after a 1 s ITI (t(95) = 5.54, p < 10⁻⁶).

table.text: Specifically, after a win, switching rose from 20.5% to 28.2% (t(95) = 5.89, p < 10⁻⁷), whereas after a loss it was unchanged (69.3% to 70.3%, t(95) = 0.61, p = 0.54; the two effects differed, t(95) = 3.54, p = 0.0006; Fig. 1d).
table.d_coherence_note: No parseable d effect size found.

:::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 308 columns across 26 data files.
#### Issues Identified

10 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 26 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

summary_table.ethics_statements: All studies were approved by the Human Subjects Institutional Review Board (HSIRB) of Bar-Ilan University (approval no. 310725687), and all participants gave informed consent online before starting the task.
live_data_statements: Thus, we used the same design as in Study 1, except here, participants completed a perceptual decisionmaking task where they needed to report whether the dominant motion of moving dots was upward or downward during the ITI to reduce any effect of replay (Fig. 2a).

In order to confirm that we used valid trials to estimate switching rates, we sought to remove trials where participants were likely still answering the perceptual task when the next choice screen appeared.

To validate these choices were in fact left-over choices from the perceptual task during the ITI, and should be discarded, we show how these choices tended to ignore the values participants had learned, unlike slower choices (Fig. 2d-f).
Choices also depended on what participants had chosen before, reflecting choice perseveration.

For each generating model, five synthetic data sets of 50 participants were simulated, each participant playing a randomly chosen real participant's task with parameters spread evenly over the full range of every parameter (Latin-hypercube sampling over the ranges of d).
We thus predicted that the ITI effect would be larger when participants were exploring options they had not recently visited and were more uncertain of.
Participants in all four studies were recruited through Prolific 31 .
They also had to report English as a fluent language and have a Prolific approval rate of 95-100%.
Each study excluded from its recruitment pool everyone who had taken part in an earlier study or pilot of the project, so no participant took part in more than one study.

All studies were approved by the Human Subjects Institutional Review Board (HSIRB) of Bar-Ilan University (approval no. 310725687), and all participants gave informed consent online before starting the task.
In Study 1, the 96 analyzed participants were aged 24 to 81 years (M = 46.2, SD = 13.0); 54 were women and 42 men.
For Studies 2 and 3, the figures below describe everyone who submitted the study on Prolific (99 and 481 people), not only the analyzed samples.
There were 246 men and 231 women, and four participants preferred not to report their sex.
Such choices were impossibly fast, did not follow the values the participant had learned and switched at the chance level of 2/3 (Fig. 2d-f).
Trials on which no response was registered within the deadline were recorded as misses, and participants were told in advance that the task would end if they accumulated five misses.
All participants were exposed to the same predetermined trajectories, so the reward probabilities changed identically, and at the same points in the task, for everyone.
Before the main task, participants completed six practice trials with a different set of images and a different set of reward trajectories, and they were told that the images would change.
Every parameter of that synthetic participant was drawn independently and uniformly over its full range, and the synthetic participants were refitted with the same hierarchy.
For model recovery among the three ITI models, five datasets of 50 synthetic participants were simulated from each model.
Thirty-one participants completed two scanned sessions of a two-armed bandit in which each ten-trial run presented a new pair of arms with fixed but unknown means, under four risk conditions.

info.title: Inter-trial intervals bias reinforcement learning in humans

text.text: Although we know humans attempt to maximize reward per unit time when foraging, it remains unclear how the common practice of varying waiting time via inter-trial intervals (ITI) impacts reinforcement learning.

Here, we tested several hypotheses concerning how time to wait during the ITI impacts reinforcement learning, including replay of recent outcomes, sensory decay of action representations, and discounting of action values due to added time costs.

To test which of these accounts explains how ITIs impact reinforcement learning, we conducted a series of bandit-style tasks in which the ITI was either 1 or 4 seconds, expecting longer ITIs to allow replay that strengthens recent learning.
Instead, across four studies (n = 96, 96, 439 and 117), a longer ITI made people more likely to change their last choice selectively after wins but not after losses.

To explain why this effect occurs, we used computational modeling to demonstrate how the ITI cost competes with learned value for control of the next choice, with time costs impacting choice more when learned values were more uncertain.
The effect of ITIs on choice generalized to a public fMRI dataset with jittered ITIs, and was absent in language-model agents playing our task.
Taken together, our results suggest that ITIs bias human reinforcement learning, where people try to reduce uncontrollable time costs through switching to a new choice.
Humans dislike waiting.
Imagine that when eating pizza, you were forced to wait for longer intervals between each bite than what you would naturally choose.
Such waiting without receiving expected reward (a tasty bite) would likely be disappointing.
This thought experiment is unusual because it contrasts with the typical scenario where, when acting in the world, we control how much reward we experience over time.

Computational work on foraging has formalized how waiting time impacts decision-making 1, 2 , wherein humans balance exploiting their current environment for reward versus exploring a new environment's potential reward by maximizing their reward per unit time 3, 4 .
text.formatted: Computational work on foraging has formalized how waiting time impacts decision-making <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2</ref> , wherein humans balance exploiting their current environment for reward versus exploring a new environment's potential reward by maximizing their reward per unit time <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref> .

text.text: The Marginal-Value Theorem provides this objective that defines optimal foraging, and explains why waiting longer without reward in one's current environment increases the opportunity cost of foregoing switching to a new environment.
Despite this seminal work on how time and reward jointly impact decision-making, the impact of waiting time on choices has been largely neglected in human reinforcement learning (RL) 5 .
text.formatted: Despite this seminal work on how time and reward jointly impact decision-making, the impact of waiting time on choices has been largely neglected in human reinforcement learning (RL) <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5</ref> .

text.text: In simple bandit-style tasks, humans make many decisions, receive rewards or punishments after those decisions, and must wait between decisions 6 .
text.formatted: In simple bandit-style tasks, humans make many decisions, receive rewards or punishments after those decisions, and must wait between decisions <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6</ref> .

text.text: Such waiting time, typically referred to as the inter-trial interval (ITI), is widely neglected as a meaningful task parameter that might alter learning and decision-making dynamics.
Indeed, as most ITIs are only on the scale of seconds, one might suspect that such small differences are overlooked by participants.

For this reason, researchers typically vary the ITI to measure neural signals that covary with latent learning variables, such as the prediction error (deviation between expected and actual outcome), without any explicit modeling or consideration as to how the range of ITIs might impact learning and decisionmaking 7, 8.
text.formatted: For this reason, researchers typically vary the ITI to measure neural signals that covary with latent learning variables, such as the prediction error (deviation between expected and actual outcome), without any explicit modeling or consideration as to how the range of ITIs might impact learning and decisionmaking <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8</ref>.

text.text: Recent work, however, does indeed suggest that waiting time impacts the learning algorithm used to make decisions.
For example, it has been shown that mice that choose their own ITIs have a different learning strategy after a chosen longer waiting time versus a shorter one 9 .
text.formatted: For example, it has been shown that mice that choose their own ITIs have a different learning strategy after a chosen longer waiting time versus a shorter one <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9</ref> .

text.text: Whereas short ITIs are followed by decisions that arise from a simple win-stay, lose-shift decision strategy, longer wait times are followed by an integrative learning rule, where mice average their expected reward for a given action over its outcome history.
In other words, longer chosen waiting time in mice reflects a normative shift toward a lower learning rate that generates expected values in line with the true reward rate.

Critically, because ITIs were chosen and not experimentally manipulated, such a finding may reflect the influence of decision strategy on the ITI rather than a causal effect of the ITI on reinforcement learning.

In humans, only longer intervals beyond the ITI, from rest periods between task phases [10] [11] [12] [13] to overnight sleep 14 , have been explored to determine how the replaying of prior experience might impact offline learning and subsequent decisions.
text.formatted: In humans, only longer intervals beyond the ITI, from rest periods between task phases <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref> to overnight sleep <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14</ref> , have been explored to determine how the replaying of prior experience might impact offline learning and subsequent decisions.

text.text: In that work, it is clear that long periods between decisions confer consolidation of prior knowledge, whereby individuals can leverage replay of prior experience to infer the latent rules and structure required to make optimal choices 12, 13.
text.formatted: In that work, it is clear that long periods between decisions confer consolidation of prior knowledge, whereby individuals can leverage replay of prior experience to infer the latent rules and structure required to make optimal choices <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13</ref>.

text.text: The impact of shorter ITIs on decision making has only been explored in tasks involving perceptual decision-making in the absence of learning.
For example, it has been shown that longer wait times dissipate recent perceptual representations, described by a representational decay model 15, 16 .
text.formatted: For example, it has been shown that longer wait times dissipate recent perceptual representations, described by a representational decay model <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16</ref> .

text.text: This has been applied to action representations, where individuals are more likely to switch to a new action after a single longer ITI 17, 18.
text.formatted: This has been applied to action representations, where individuals are more likely to switch to a new action after a single longer ITI <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18</ref>.

text.text: Despite this important work, it remains unclear whether in human RL tasks, one would see evidence of replay of recent outcomes, of action-representation decay, or of time costs entering the valuation of actions, as a function of longer ITIs.
Unlike existing replay work, the ITIs in typical RL experiments are much shorter, and they are interrupted by ongoing task experience.
On the other hand, unlike perceptual decision making work, typical RL tasks involve non-independent trials that require participants to learn the latent reward structure.

And, ultimately, the only work to assess how time-costs impact the value of decisions comes from foraging paradigms, which do not involve the multi-action choice problem endemic to reinforcement learning.

To address these gaps in order to determine the impact of waiting time on learning and decision making, we sought to assess how experimentally varying the ITI (1 or 4 seconds) impacts how humans learn in bandit-style tasks used in human RL.

Although originally hypothesizing that we would see evidence of greater replay under longer ITIs, we instead discovered that humans are biased to switch to new choices after longer ITIs, particularly after a reward.

We then replicated these findings in three independent datasets using the same task, showed that our core finding generalized to an existing fMRI dataset, and demonstrated that AI models do not exhibit the same key effect of ITI on choice.

To explain the mechanism giving rise to this behavior, we developed a computational model that explains how humans act like foragers in RL tasks, treating the time spent waiting after an action as a cost of that action.

The time cost during a long wait competes with the learned value of each option for control of the next choice, selectively weakening the reinforcement of a rewarded action, explaining whylonger waits increased switching after wins and not after losses.
The shift was also strongest when the last choice was exploratory, that is, when learned values were most uncertain.

We regard such switching behavior as a bias because the ITIs in the task were random with respect to choices, and thus choosing to switch to a new action did not on average result in shorter waiting time.
Below, we describe the series of studies that evidences this model where time and value compete for behavioral control during RL.
In doing so, we rule out compelling alternative replay, sensory decay and value-time integrated learning accounts of the impact of ITIs on reinforcement learning.

We tested how ITIs might impact learning and decision-making in a three-armed bandit task (Fig. 1) in four separate studies (Study 1, n = 96; Study 2, n = 96; Study 3, preregistered, n = 439; Study 4, preregistered, n = 117).
text.formatted: We tested how ITIs might impact learning and decision-making in a three-armed bandit task (Fig. <ref type="figure">1</ref>) in four separate studies (Study 1, n = 96; Study 2, n = 96; Study 3, preregistered, n = 439; Study 4, preregistered, n = 117).

text.text: Our initial hypothesis concerned the potential role replay might play during ITIs.
Specifically, we expected that, if given more time to think during the ITI, offline learning over one's remembered action-outcome sequences might augment the rate of learning for recent outcomes.
For example, if experiencing a positive outcome, longer ITI would increase the tendency to stay with one's prior action due to recencyweighted sampling of memory.
Indeed, prior research suggests that offline learning over remembered outcomes facilitates learning, and is biased by recent outcomes 10, 19.
text.formatted: Indeed, prior research suggests that offline learning over remembered outcomes facilitates learning, and is biased by recent outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19</ref>.

text.text: In contrast to our initial hypothesis, results showed that longer ITI increased switching behavior.
In Study 1, participants switched away from the option they had just chosen on 45.1% of trials after a 4 s ITI versus 38.9% after a 1 s ITI (t(95) = 5.54, p < 10⁻⁶).
text.formatted: In Study 1, participants switched away from the option they had just chosen on 45.1% of trials after a 4 s ITI versus 38.9% after a 1 s ITI (t(95) = 5.54, p < 10⁻⁶).

text.text: In fact, the effect was larger after a win, suggesting that replaying the last outcome to induce offline learning was not evident.

Specifically, after a win, switching rose from 20.5% to 28.2% (t(95) = 5.89, p < 10⁻⁷), whereas after a loss it was unchanged (69.3% to 70.3%, t(95) = 0.61, p = 0.54; the two effects differed, t(95) = 3.54, p = 0.0006; Fig. 1d).
text.formatted: Specifically, after a win, switching rose from 20.5% to 28.2% (t(95) = 5.89, p < 10⁻⁷), whereas after a loss it was unchanged (69.3% to 70.3%, t(95) = 0.61, p = 0.54; the two effects differed, t(95) = 3.54, p = 0.0006; Fig. <ref type="figure">1d</ref>).

text.text: To see whether the effect was robust to timebound influences, such as the shift from early to late learning and fatigue, we also tested it early and late in the task, in the first and second half of the trials (trials 2-50 and 51-100; Fig. 1e): after a win, switching rose from 26.8% to 32.5% in the first half (t(95) = 3.16, p = 0.002) and from 17.8% to 23.5% in the second (t(95) = 4.05, p < 10⁻³), whereas after a loss it did not change in either half (73.9% to 72.6%, t(95) = 0.67, p = 0.51; 65.2% to 66.4%, t(95) = 0.51, p = 0.61).
text.formatted: To see whether the effect was robust to timebound influences, such as the shift from early to late learning and fatigue, we also tested it early and late in the task, in the first and second half of the trials (trials 2-50 and 51-100; Fig. <ref type="figure">1e</ref>): after a win, switching rose from 26.8% to 32.5% in the first half (t(95) = 3.16, p = 0.002) and from 17.8% to 23.5% in the second (t(95) = 4.05, p < 10⁻³), whereas after a loss it did not change in either half (73.9% to 72.6%, t(95) = 0.67, p = 0.51; 65.2% to 66.4%, t(95) = 0.51, p = 0.61).

text.text: Despite this bias, participants learned overall, choosing the option with the highest current reward probability on 47% of trials, against 33% expected by chance (t(95) = 15.7, p < 10⁻²⁷; Fig. 1c).
text.formatted: Despite this bias, participants learned overall, choosing the option with the highest current reward probability on 47% of trials, against 33% expected by chance (t(95) = 15.7, p < 10⁻²⁷; Fig. <ref type="figure">1c</ref>).

As in prior work on offline replay, a demanding secondary task reduces replay of past experiences 20 .

text.text: In order to confirm that we used valid trials to estimate switching rates, we sought to remove trials where participants were likely still answering the perceptual task when the next choice screen appeared.

A downward trial was answered by pressing Q, T and P together, the three keys used to choose any bandit, and when the display ended before the press, the press landed on the choice screen, where the first of the three keys to go down registered as a choice.
After a missed downward display at 1 s, 24% of the next choices came within 250 ms (likely too fast) of the choice screen and 8% within 50 ms.

To validate these choices were in fact left-over choices from the perceptual task during the ITI, and should be discarded, we show how these choices tended to ignore the values participants had learned, unlike slower choices (Fig. 2d-f).

text.text: We next sought to preregister our key hypothesis in a large, online sample in order to both ensure findings generalize and to determine whether any individual differences moderate the effect.
We confirmed in these data that, as hypothesized, switching rose after long ITIs (46.0% to 51.9%, t(438) = 12.30, p < 10⁻²⁹).

text.text: Moreover, as in the two previous studies, the effect was significant after wins (29.3% to 36.5%, t(438) = 12.30, p < 10⁻²⁹) and not significant after losses (71.8% to 72.9%, t(438) = 1.74, p = 0.083; Fig. 3a).

text.text: Before asking what mechanism produces the bias, we first had to rule out an artifact specific to our design that we discovered while analyzing the data in Study 3.
Switching is not stationary, likely due to participants' uncertainty varying over the task [21] [22] [23] .
text.formatted: Switching is not stationary, likely due to participants' uncertainty varying over the task <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23]</ref> .

text.text: Indeed, in Study 3, switching fell from 62% in the first twenty trials (likely where participants explore to reduce uncertainty) to 40% in the last twenty, steeply at first and then more slowly (Fig. 3c).
text.formatted: Indeed, in Study 3, switching fell from 62% in the first twenty trials (likely where participants explore to reduce uncertainty) to 40% in the last twenty, steeply at first and then more slowly (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">3c</ref>).

text.text: This trend in switching happened to coincide with our random sequence-generation of ITIs, where 4-second ITIs happened to be more likely at the start of the task.
We therefore asked whether the ITI effect survives once this decline in switching over trials is modeled.
We fitted the preregistered mixed-effects logistic regression of switching on the preceding ITI with trial number added as both a fixed and random (by participant) effect.
After controlling for this declining trend, the ITI effect on switching held in Study 3 (b = 0.040, CI = [0.025, 0.055]).
Every test of the ITI below uses this mixed-effects model with its linear trial term.
Testing the effect early and late in the task, as in Studies 1 and 2, supports the same conclusion without relying on the trial term.
The confound lies in the first half of the session: the first forty trials held 70% and 60% long ITIs, and this is where switching, and presumably exploration, was highest.

From trial 41 on, the sequence placed 40% long ITIs in every block of twenty trials and switching had largely leveled off, so that in the second half (trials 51-100) long ITIs and early exploration no longer coincided (correlation between a long ITI and trial number 0.05, against 0.15 in the first half).

The post-win effect was present there as -well: after a win, switching rose from 27.4% to 32.3% after a long ITI (t(438) = 7.10, p < 10⁻¹¹), close to its size in the first half (33.4% to 40.3%, t(438) = 8.37, p < 10⁻¹⁵), whereas after a loss there was no effect in either half (75.4% to 75.4%, t(438) = 0.03, p = 0.97; 69.4% to 67.8%, t(438) = 1.80, p = 0.07; Fig. 3b).
text.formatted: The post-win effect was present there as -well: after a win, switching rose from 27.4% to 32.3% after a long ITI (t(438) = 7.10, p < 10⁻¹¹), close to its size in the first half (33.4% to 40.3%, t(438) = 8.37, p < 10⁻¹⁵), whereas after a loss there was no effect in either half (75.4% to 75.4%, t(438) = 0.03, p = 0.97; 69.4% to 67.8%, t(438) = 1.80, p = 0.07; Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">3b</ref>).

text.text: The effect after wins therefore does not depend on the part of the session in which early exploration and long ITIs were confounded.
To determine the underlying mechanism giving rise to our replicated ITI effect, we formulated three classes of models that each make unique behavioral predictions.

The first, inspired by resource-rational and foraging accounts of decision-making, treats time as a cost: the value of an action combines its expected reward, which is to be maximized, and its expected waiting time, the ITI, which is to be reduced.
If this were in fact true, then participants should be more willing to abandon actions that have recently been followed by longer ITIs.
However, there could be various ways in which the ITI cost impacts choices.
If the wait is simply subtracted from the reward it follows, its effect (on the log-odds scale) should be equivalent after a win and a loss.
If instead the ITI cost competes with learned value for control over the next choice, its impact aligns with that of a loss but is at-odds with that of a win.
An asymmetry between wins and losses is therefore the signature that separates these two ways in which ITI costs and learned values are integrated in the learning process (Methods).
The second account of how time might bias decision-making draws inspiration from perceptual decision-making, where time decays biases to choose the last action taken.
This inherently is value-independent, and thus should act not on a value representation, but on choice perseveration.
Thus, regardless of whether a win or loss occurred, the bias in switching after a long ITI should be the same.

Finally, a third possibility is that participants learn how long waits are in the task as a whole, and that this global expectation, rather than the wait that followed the last action, drives switching.
Unlike the other two, it predicts that an earlier ITI should affect the tendency to take actions other than the action preceding it.
We first sought to rule out the global ITI cost account, which on its face is a less sensible foraging-like strategy than treating each action as its own environment.
Specifically, if global time inherently treats all actions as belonging to a single environment, switching cannot reduce time costs (one is still switching within the same environment).

We thus tested whether the key prediction of this account was present in the current data, wherein a long ITI after an earlier choice should raise the tendency to leave a different action than the one preceding that prior ITI.
By comparing trials on which the option chosen two trials back differed from the option chosen last, we asked whether the ITI that followed that earlier choice predicted current-trial switching.
A global account predicts that this earlier ITI should raise switching much as the last one does.
Like the main effect, this test inherits the decline in switching over trials, so we used the same mixed-effects model with its linear trial term.
The earlier ITI did not predict switching in Study 3 (b = 0.025, CI = [ 0.040, 0.090]), and neither did the ITIs after the choices three and four trials back (Supplementary Fig. 1).
text.formatted: The earlier ITI did not predict switching in Study 3 (b = 0.025, CI = [ 0.040, 0.090]), and neither did the ITIs after the choices three and four trials back (Supplementary Fig. <ref type="figure">1</ref>).

text.text: Switching depends on the ITI just elapsed and not on earlier ones, so we found no model-agnostic signature of a global expectation.
The ITI-on-choice-bias account, by contrast, makes a prediction about the previous choice irrespective of the reward that came after it.
Thus, the effect of a longer ITI should raise switching after a win and after a loss alike (Fig. 3d, middle).
text.formatted: Thus, the effect of a longer ITI should raise switching after a win and after a loss alike (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">3d</ref>, middle).

text.text: In contrast to this prediction in Study 3, the long ITI raised the odds of switching after wins (odds ratio 1.44, CI = [1.33, 1.56]) and not after losses (0.95, CI = [0.88, 1.02]; ITI × outcome interaction b = 0.145, CI = [0.112, 0.178]).
Such an asymmetry is predicted when the ITI competes with value for control of the next choice.

To specify exactly how value and time effects are integrated to impact choice behavior, we formalized a series of computational models in which reward and time were either integrated in a combined learning target (additive time cost) or as separate and competing influences on their associated action. a, Switching after a 1 s and after a 4 s ITI, after a win and after a loss (n = 439; mean ± s.e.m. across participants; paired t tests). b, The same contrast in the first and the second half of the session (trials 2-50 and 51-100; mean ± s.e.m. across participants; paired t tests). c, Probability of switching on every trial (mean ± s.e.m. across participants), colored by the ITI that preceded that trial (red, 4 s; blue, 1 s), with a 9-trial moving average (black).

To test these mechanistic accounts of the ITI impact on learning and choice, we built a series of reinforcement-learning models fitted to choice data in Study 3, the preregistered study with the largest sample.

Each component was kept only if it improved out-of-sample predictive accuracy, and each addition to the model was simulated to show it can produce its intended qualitative signature of behavior that real participants displayed (Methods; Fig. 4a,b; Supplementary Table 1).

text.text: Models were fitted as hierarchical Bayesian models and compared by Paretosmoothed importance-sampling leave-one-out cross-validation, summarized by the expected log predictive density (ELPD).
Our model comparison first established that that participants did indeed learn from outcomes, and thus are sensitive to the value of choices.
A Rescorla-Wagner learner predicted choices far better than fixed preferences for the three options (ELPD difference +7,518, SE 121).
Separate learning rates for wins and losses improved it further (+346, SE 35), and so did value decay, which lets the values of unchosen options drift back toward a neutral prior (+1,575, SE 66).
The learning models also resembled choices better than models with a constant intercept fit to each choice (root-mean-square error 0.035 to 0.042, against 0.068; Fig. 4b).
text.formatted: The learning models also resembled choices better than models with a constant intercept fit to each choice (root-mean-square error 0.035 to 0.042, against 0.068; Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">4b</ref>).

text.text: Choices also depended on what participants had chosen before, reflecting choice perseveration.

We compared two ways of capturing this, each added to the value learner: a constant bias toward repeating the option chosen last, and a choice kernel, which keeps a running trace of how often each option has been chosen recently and adds it, weighted, to the decision value of every option 24 .
text.formatted: We compared two ways of capturing this, each added to the value learner: a constant bias toward repeating the option chosen last, and a choice kernel, which keeps a running trace of how often each option has been chosen recently and adds it, weighted, to the decision value of every option <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">24</ref> .

text.text: The choice kernel fit choices better (+717.3 over the value-decay model, SE 42.7, against +634.1, SE 33.8, for the constant stay bias; difference +83.2, SE 48.4), yet neither fully reproduced how much more often participants switched after a switch than after a stay (Fig. 4b) which left added variance to explain switching behavior.
text.formatted: The choice kernel fit choices better (+717.3 over the value-decay model, SE 42.7, against +634.1, SE 33.8, for the constant stay bias; difference +83.2, SE 48.4), yet neither fully reproduced how much more often participants switched after a switch than after a stay (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">4b</ref>) which left added variance to explain switching behavior.

text.text: Switching was in part strategic.
Only 38.6% of the switches returned to the most recently chosen alternative (50% if they had chosen at random between the two alternatives), whereas the choice-kernel model predicted 51.7%.
Participants instead tended to switch to the option they had chosen furthest back.
A novelty bonus for that option was added, which improved qualitative model predictions (Fig. 4b), and model fit (+913.7, SE 44.4).
text.formatted: A novelty bonus for that option was added, which improved qualitative model predictions (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">4b</ref>), and model fit (+913.7, SE 44.4).

text.text: Switching also declined over trials, which likely reflected that general task uncertainty fell over the course of learning.
To model declining uncertainty, we added a parameter which allowed the inverse temperature to change log-linearly over trials, which improved performance (+559.8, SE 35.7).
This fit better than allowing a decreasing trend in the weight of the choice kernel, which improved on the novelty model by only +114.7 (SE 15.7; difference between the two trends +445.1, SE 37.0).
Qualitatively, the model with a dynamic inverse temperature also followed the decline in switching more closely (Fig. 4b).

The effect of the ITI on switching (the probability after a 4 s ITI minus after a 1 s ITI) by quintile of u = 1/(1 + n) for the option chosen on the trial before the ITI (n, a count of the option's earlier choices that grows by one when it is chosen and loses a fraction 0.85 of its size on every trial it is not; quintiles within participant and outcome, 1 most exploitative, 5 most exploratory), after a win and after a loss, in Studies 3 and 4.
To ultimately determine how ITIs impacted switching behavior, we first asked whether the effect of longer ITIs on choice varied with any task feature prior to fitting a new model.
We hypothesized that the ITI effect might be stronger when value learning is a less reliable source of evidence.
We thus predicted that the ITI effect would be larger when participants were exploring options they had not recently visited and were more uncertain of.

As a model-agnostic proxy for exploratory versus exploitative state we quantified how exploratory the option chosen on the trial before the ITI was as u = 1/(1 + n), where n counts the option's earlier choices (Methods; the proxy is consistent with the explore and exploit states of a hidden Markov model of choices).

After wins, the effect of the ITI grew with u (Fig. 4f), from +0.048 in the most exploitative quintile of each participant's trials to +0.083 in the most exploratory quintile (per-participant trend across quintiles, t(438) = 3.41, p = 0.0007).
text.formatted: After wins, the effect of the ITI grew with u (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">4f</ref>), from +0.048 in the most exploitative quintile of each participant's trials to +0.083 in the most exploratory quintile (per-participant trend across quintiles, t(438) = 3.41, p = 0.0007).

text.text: After losses it rose only from 0.036 to 0.001 --(t(438) = 2.01, p = 0.045).
These results suggest that the ITI impacts choice most when value is a less reliable guide for choice.
We therefore compared three ways in which the ITI could enter the model (Methods).

In the first, the ITI-as-learning-target model (an additive time cost), the long wait that followed an outcome is subtracted from the value learned from it, by the same amount after a win and after a loss.
In the second, the ITI-onchoice-bias model, the ITI is insensitive to value and modulates the choice-bias term.
The third, the ITI-competes-with-value model, was built on the prior exploration result.
When people explore, their choices are by definition less governed by learned value, and random exploration is commonly modeled as a lower weight on value 6, 22 .
text.formatted: When people explore, their choices are by definition less governed by learned value, and random exploration is commonly modeled as a lower weight on value <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22</ref> .

text.text: In this model the weight of a decision is shared between two sources of evidence.
One is the learned value of each option, and the other is the ITI just experienced, which counts against the option chosen before it.
After a long ITI, part of the weight moves from value to the wait.
The share that moves grows with how exploratory that choice was (u = 1/(1 + n), with n here the number of times in a row the option had just been chosen; Methods).
Because the total weight is fixed, whatever exploration takes from value goes to time.

Importantly, in all models, we used only the last ITI, and not a running estimate of expected ITI, given model-agnostic evidence that only the last ITI predicted current choices (Supplementary Note 1; Supplementary Fig. 2).
text.formatted: Importantly, in all models, we used only the last ITI, and not a running estimate of expected ITI, given model-agnostic evidence that only the last ITI predicted current choices (Supplementary Note 1; Supplementary Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">2</ref>).

text.text: We then compared the three ITI models with the model without an ITI term and with each other (Fig. 4a).

text.text: In Study 3 the ITI-competes-with-value model was the best model overall.
It improved on the model without an ITI term by 118.2 (SE 16.8), on the ITI-as-learning-target model by 104.1 (SE 16.9) and on the ITI-onchoice-bias model by 110.9 (SE 16.5).
The ITI-as-learning-target model itself improved on the model without an ITI term by 14.1 (SE 8.7), and the ITI-on-choicebias model by 7.3 (SE 5.3).
As a sensitivity analysis to the ELPD comparison, random-effects Bayesian model selection also favored the ITI-competes-with-value model (protected exceedance probability, PXP > 0.99).
text.formatted: As a sensitivity analysis to the ELPD comparison, random-effects Bayesian model selection also favored the ITI-competes-with-value model (protected exceedance probability, PXP > 0.99).

text.text: In this model, a long ITI after a switch to an option moved a share κ = 0.096 (CI = [0.066, 0.126]) of the weight of the next decision from value to the wait.
The share halved after two choices of the option in a row and fell further after longer runs.
The ITI terms of the other two models were small.
A long ITI weakened the choice bias (γ = 0.097, CI = [ 0.169, 0.030]) or lowered the --value learned from the outcome before it (c = 0.060, CI = [0.027, 0.094], on outcomes coded ±1).

The winning model, although containing 9 parameters, had good parameter recovery (Fig. 4d), including specifically the ITI weight κ recovered with r = 0.80 (0.59 within the range of the fitted participant estimates) and the other parameters with r from 0.65 (the learning rate after a win) to 0.92 (the novelty bonus).

text.text: It thus reproduced the asymmetry between outcomes without a parameter for the outcome.
The ITI-competes-with-value model was also the only model whose effect after wins grew with exploratory state (Fig. 4f), with no such trend after losses.

text.text: Response times, which the models were not fitted to, showed the same asymmetry as choices, as the ITI-competes-with-value model predicts.

In Study 3, after a win a long ITI slowed staying relative to switching (interaction of ITI and stay on log response time, +0.052, CI = [0.035, 0.069]), and after a loss it did not ( 0.019, CI = -[ 0.040, 0.001]; three-way interaction of ITI, stay and outcome +0.073, CI = [0.047, -0.100]; Bayesian linear mixed model with trial number as a fixed effect and participant random slope).

To assess individual differences, we hypothesized and preregistered that trait impulsivity would be positively associated with the effect of time on choice, given that they may have higher opportunity costs to foregoing new opportunities in their environment, and anhedonia would show the opposite effect.
Neither preregistered test was supported (impulsivity r(437) = 0.05, one-sided p = 0.16; anhedonia r(437) = 0.02 in the wrong direction, one-sided p = 0.62).

An exploratory analysis restricted to post-win trials, where the effect is concentrated, found a small positive association with impulsivity (r(437) = 0.11, p = 0.023; Spearman ρ(437) = 0.13, p = 0.008), which does not survive controlling for the decline in switching over trials (each participant's ITI slope from the mixed-effects model with the linear trial term: r(437) = 0.08, p = 0.11).
To test whether our findings generalize to existing similar studies, we first showed that our main effect was replicable in an independent dataset without the ITI-bytrial confound.
Specifically, in a new Study 4, we expected that the ITI effect would be stronger after a win than after a loss even when longer ITIs were no longer more common toward the start of the experiment.

We ran the task of Study 3 unchanged except for the fixed sequence of ITIs, which was constructed against the hypothesis: 26 of the 50 ITIs in the first half of the task were short and 26 of the 50 in the second half long, with five or six short ITIs in every block of ten trials in the first half and the mirror image in the second (Fig. 5c).

text.text: Long ITIs were therefore no longer concentrated where switching is highest.

Participants learned as before (chose-best rate 0.45, t(116) = 13.7, p < 10⁻²⁵) and switching declined as before, from 63% over the first twenty trials to 41% over the last twenty (withinparticipant slope 0.26 per 100 trials, t(116) = 8.1, p < 10 --⁻¹²).

text.text: The response-time pattern replicated as well: after a win a long ITI slowed staying relative to switching (ITI × stay, +0.069, CI = [0.037, 0.100]), whereas after a loss the shift went the other way ( 0.061, CI = [ 0.100, 0.021]; three-way interaction +0.128, CI = [0.079, ---0.178]).
As in Studies 1-3, the ITI after the choice two trials back did not predict switching when that option differed from the last one (odds ratio 0.93, CI = [0.83, 1.06]; Supplementary Fig. 2).

text.text: The computational modeling of Study 4 mirrored that of Study 3 (see Supplemental Material), wherein the ITI-competes-with-value model was again the best-fitting model.
Simulated from its fitted parameters, the winning model was again the only model whose effect after wins grew with exploratory state (Fig 4f).

text.text: To demonstrate that our key hypothesis generalizes to existing studies, and was not a produce of our task-design choices, we sought to determine whether the key prediction of our model would be replicated in a publicly shared fMRI dataset.

We chose the two-armed bandit of Tomov et al. 25 , in which 31 participants played a new pair of arms every ten trials over two scanned sessions, because its ITIs cover a range of similar width to ours (about 2.5 s, from 4.8 to 7.3 s), though shifted toward the longer intervals typical of fMRI, and are sampled uniformly across that range, which lets us estimate a continuous slope relating ITI length to choice switching.
text.formatted: We chose the two-armed bandit of Tomov et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25</ref> , in which 31 participants played a new pair of arms every ten trials over two scanned sessions, because its ITIs cover a range of similar width to ours (about 2.5 s, from 4.8 to 7.3 s), though shifted toward the longer intervals typical of fMRI, and are sampled uniformly across that range, which lets us estimate a continuous slope relating ITI length to choice switching.

text.text: In a Bayesian mixed-effects model with participant-level random intercepts, ITI slopes and linear trends over the ten trials of each pair of arms, a longer ITI before the choice increased switching (b = 0.130 log-odds per second, CI = [0.004, 0.255]; posterior probability of a positive slope 0.98; Fig. 6a).

text.text: The effect of the ITI on switching thus held in an independent dataset.

Ultimately, to ensure our effects were not biased by online dissemination, we asked whether online artificial agents might have been responsible for our findings, a documented and growing concern in online samples 26, 27 .

text.text: We reasoned that leading models would not show our key result, because the effect of ITIs on reinforcement learning is absent from the literature these models are trained on and so is unlikely to be part of their imitation of human behavior.

To test the hypothesis that LLMs would not display our key behavior, we had large language models (Claude Opus 5, Sonnet 5 and Haiku 4.5) play the Study 4 task through the live web page as naive participants 28, 29 .

text.text: Each agent was a fresh conversation that saw only what a participant sees: the text of every screen from the consent form to the questionnaires, the outcome of each choice ("You won $1" or "You lost $1") and a screenshot of the task screen on its first practice trial and its first task trial.
It had no access to the page's code or to the reward probabilities, and every prompt it received was logged.
The trial order, outcomes and ITI sequence were exactly those of Study 4, and the ITI was described in words.
We tried several AI agents with different prompts and information regarding what the ITI was each trial and whether time might matter or not in this task.
In the time-blind condition, the agent was not told the ITI.
By contrast, in the time-told condition, the ITI was named ("shown for 4 seconds").
We also varied our attempt to promote human mimicry in behavior, by saying, in the opening instructions either "Play like a human would", or "Play like a human that is sensitive to time costs."
Fourteen agents were run (six instruction × condition cells of one to three agents; total cost about $7).
The agents learned the task at least as well as people (Fig. 6f), yet also overexploited relative to humans (Fig. 6e).

text.text: The post-win ITI effect that all four human studies show was not reflected in the agents' behavior.
After wins the difference between 4 s and 1 s lay between 0.03 and +0.01 regardless of how we prompted the agents to pay attention to time in the task (Fig. 6c).
